title: How Coffee Was Discovered
summary: Tells the story of how coffee was discovered, from a legend about a goat herder in Africa noticing his goats' energy after eating wild berries, to people roasting and grinding the beans, opening lively coffee houses, and traders eventually spreading coffee across the world.
poll: The discovery and spread of coffee changed daily life for people around the world.

versions.title: How Coffee Was Discovered
versions.text:
Long ago, coffee plants grew wild. They grew in a far land. The plants grew small red berries. Each one had two seeds. We call these seeds coffee beans.

A story tells of a man. He had some goats. His goats ate the small red fruit. The goats then felt full of pep. The man tried some too.

Word of this fruit spread far. Folks in a new land grew the plant. They cooked the beans with fire. This made the beans turn brown.

Workers then ground up the beans. They mixed the ground beans with hot water. This drink became known as coffee. People drank it more and more.

Coffee shops opened in big towns. Folks met there to talk. They played games and shared news. These shops became popular spots.

Traders took coffee beans far away. It reached new lands over time. Today, folks all over drink coffee.

versions.text:
For many generations, coffee plants grew wild in a remote region of Africa, far from any established cities or trade routes connecting distant communities, and these plants produced small red berries scattered across their branches throughout much of the year, ripening gradually and unevenly depending on local conditions, rainfall, and elevation. Each berry held two seeds tucked safely inside its soft outer flesh, protected from the elements until carefully harvested by hand. We now refer to these seeds as coffee beans, the basis of a beverage enjoyed throughout the entire modern world today.

An enduring legend tells of a goat herder who reportedly lived many centuries ago somewhere within that region, and his goats supposedly consumed some small red fruit growing from a particular bush one otherwise ordinary afternoon without warning. The goats then seemed unusually energetic afterward, bouncing around with surprising vigor and enthusiasm that caught his attention immediately and completely. The herder, intrigued by this unexpected behavior, decided to sample the strange fruit himself out of genuine curiosity about its mysterious effects.

Word of this remarkable fruit eventually spread to neighboring lands and regions across a considerably wider geographic area, and people in a different locality began cultivating the plant themselves soon after hearing these intriguing accounts passed along by travelers and merchants alike. They roasted the harvested beans over open fire until the beans gradually darkened into a deep, rich brown, a process that gave the beans a noticeably stronger, more complex aroma than the raw fruit ever possessed.

Skilled workers then carefully ground the freshly roasted beans using simple hand tools available at the time, and they combined the resulting ground beans with hot, steaming water to produce a dark, flavorful beverage enjoyed by a great many people. This novel drink soon became widely recognized simply as coffee throughout the broader region, and people gradually incorporated it into their daily routines, drinking it with increasing regularity and genuine, lasting enthusiasm.

Coffee houses soon emerged in busy, crowded towns and cities throughout the region, drawing remarkably diverse crowds together from every walk of life imaginable, and people gathered there regularly to converse, reflect, and unwind together following a demanding day's labor. Patrons played games there and freely exchanged the latest local news and gossip, and these establishments quickly became popular, lively gathering spots central to community life.

Merchants carried coffee beans across considerable distances via both overland and maritime trade routes, and coffee gradually reached numerous new, distant lands over the following centuries of expanding global commerce and rich cultural exchange. Today, people across the entire world happily consume coffee as part of their everyday lives, year after year.

MID.prompt: Explain how coffee went from a wild plant to a drink enjoyed in coffee houses around the world. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: Coffee began as a wild plant growing in a remote region, where, according to legend, a goat herder noticed his goats seemed unusually energetic after eating red berries, which led him to try the fruit out of curiosity. People in nearby regions then began growing the plant themselves, roasting the beans over fire and grinding them to mix with hot water. Coffee houses soon opened in busy towns, becoming popular spots where people gathered to talk and share news. Traders then carried coffee beans across long distances by land and sea, which helped coffee gradually reach many new, distant lands.

HIGH.prompt: The article relies on a legend about a goat herder to explain coffee's discovery, even though it may not be fully verified as historical fact. Do you think it is appropriate for articles about history to include legends like this one? Support your answer with evidence from the article, and address at least one point someone might raise against your view.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the question.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one counterpoint.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think it is appropriate for articles about history to include legends like this one, as long as they are clearly identified as legends, which this article does. The article presents the goat herder's story as an enduring legend rather than a confirmed fact, which lets readers enjoy a memorable explanation for coffee's discovery while understanding it may not be entirely accurate. Someone might argue that including unverified legends in a factual article risks confusing readers about what is proven and what is simply a popular story. That is a fair concern, but the article addresses it by clearly labeling the goat herder's tale as a legend rather than presenting it as settled history, which allows readers to appreciate the story's cultural value without mistaking it for verified fact.
